title: Making a strong password you can remember

explain.say: Your password is like the key to your house. Would you hide your key under the doormat where everyone looks first? Let us make a key that is hard to guess but easy for you to remember. Look at the board: weak on one side, strong on the other.

draw.text: Making a strong password you can remember

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Long and random beats short and clever

explain.say: Look at the weak side. Your name, your pet or your birthday are easy for anyone to find. And computers can try millions of common passwords every second. Which of your details could a stranger find online?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Long and random beats short and clever

explain.say: Now the strong side. The trick is length. Pick three random words that do not go together, like tiger, mango and kite, join them up, and add a number or symbol. Long, random and easy to picture! Can you imagine a silly picture for your three words?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Long and random beats short and clever

explain.say: Watch how much harder each one is to guess. A 4 digit PIN has 10 thousand choices. Six small letters have about 300 million. Three random words have hundreds of billions! See the last tower? Why does adding one more word help so much?

items.label: 3 random words

explain.say: Brilliant! Two more golden rules: use a different password for each app, and never share it, even with friends. Turn on two-step login too, so a code on your phone is also needed. Wow fact: four random words give over 3 thousand million million choices!

faq.a: A password is weak if it is short, common, or easy to find out, like your name, birthday, pet, 123456 or password. Using the same one everywhere is also risky.
asks: Why should I not use my birthday as a password?

faq.a: Length and randomness. A long passphrase of three or more random words, with a number or symbol, is strong and still easy to remember.
asks: How do I make a strong password?

faq.q: Why are long passwords harder to guess?
faq.a: Each extra character or word multiplies the number of possible passwords. Three random words from a list of about 7776 give around 470 billion choices, far more than any short password.
asks: Is a long password better than a complex one?
How long should a password be?

faq.q: Is it OK to use the same password everywhere?
faq.a: No. If one website is hacked, criminals try that password on your other accounts. Use a different one for each, and a password manager or a grown-up can help you keep track.

Two-step login, also called two-factor authentication, asks for a second proof, like a code sent to your phone, as well as your password. Even if someone learns your password, they still cannot get in.

facts: The UK National Cyber Security Centre recommends passwords made of three random words.
